beats.say: On August 14, 1947, a British technician installed a concealed 35mm camera inside a Punjab freight wagon.
beats.visual: British railway freight wagon Punjab 1947 interior

beats.say: The lens caught refugees clutching family heirlooms as the midnight train screeched toward the new border.
Among the passengers, a young Sikh woman whispered the name of her lost village, Mirpur, before the shutter clicked.
The footage later surfaced in a 1950s British newsreel, edited to show orderly migrations, masking the chaos.
When the reels were digitized in 2018, uncut scenes showed violent clashes at the Wagah crossing, never aired.
One frame captures a British officer ordering troops to fire on a crowd of terrified women holding newborns.
The same reel reveals a hidden inscription on a railcar: 'For the Empire's record - 1947'.
Scholars now use these clips to argue that the official narrative of a peaceful split was a post-war fabrication.
The secret camera's legacy forces us to reread history through the eyes of those who survived the horror.
